name: Battle of Leipzig
info: The armies of the Sixth Coalition, from Austria, Prussia, Sweden and Russia, defeated Napoleon's Grande Armée at Leipzig in Saxony over four days in October 1813, and the French withdrew to France.

facts.place: Leipzig, Saxony, in present-day Germany, between the Pleiße and the Parthe rivers
facts.sides: The Sixth Coalition (Russia, Austria, Prussia and Sweden), led by Tsar Alexander I, Karl von Schwarzenberg, Gebhard von Blücher and Crown Prince Charles John of Sweden, with around 380,000 troops and 1,500 guns; the French under Napoleon, with around 198,000 troops, or up to 225,000 by other estimates, including Poles, Italians and Germans of the Confederation of the Rhine
facts.outcome: The Coalition decisively defeated Napoleon, who was compelled to return to France. Estimates of the total killed, wounded or missing range from 80,000 to 110,000.

t: Leipzig was the largest battle of the Napoleonic Wars, with about 560,000 soldiers, 2,200 artillery pieces and 133,000 casualties, and arguably the deciding battle of the wars.
Most of Napoleon's army consisted of teenagers and inexperienced conscripts, and Saxon and Württemberg troops went over to the Coalition during the fighting.
After the battle the Confederation of the Rhine was dissolved, the Coalition invaded France in early 1814, and Napoleon abdicated on 6 April.
dyk: On 19 October a corporal ignited the fuses of the only bridge over the Elster at 1:00 in the afternoon, while it was still crowded with retreating French troops. Marshal Poniatowski, wounded, was among those who drowned.
ev: Napoleon invades Russia with around 685,000 troops and the Grande Armée is virtually destroyed in the retreat
Napoleon wins at Lützen and Bautzen, and a brief armistice follows
Austria joins the Coalition and the Trachenberg Plan is set, though Napoleon wins at Dresden on 27 August
Oudinot is beaten at Großbeeren and Ney at Dennewitz, and Napoleon withdraws westward to organise his forces around Leipzig
The fighting at Leipzig begins on 16 October on the southern and northern fronts and ends in a draw
On 18 October the Coalition encircles Napoleon's army and Saxon troops defect, and that night he begins the retreat
On 19 October the Elster bridge is blown while the French cross it, and Leipzig falls to the Coalition
The Coalition invades France, Paris falls on 31 March, and Napoleon abdicates on 6 April

sections.background:
Napoleon invaded Russia on 24 June 1812 with around 685,000 troops and entered Moscow in late 1812 after the bloody yet indecisive Battle of Borodino. Alexander I refused to surrender, and the campaign ended in disaster as the French retreated through the Russian winter, with sickness, starvation and the harrying of Cossacks and partisans. The Grande Armée was virtually destroyed by the time it returned. In June 1813 the combined armies of Portugal, Spain and the United Kingdom under Wellington routed the French at Vitoria. The Sixth Coalition formed, comprising Prussia, Russia, Spain, Portugal, Sweden, the United Kingdom and smaller German states whose citizens and leaders were no longer loyal to Napoleon.

Napoleon raised another large army, mostly raw and young conscripts, and sought to regain the offensive in Germany. He won hard-fought tactical victories at Lützen on 2 May and Bautzen on 20–21 May, and a brief armistice followed. During it the monarchs of Russia and Prussia met Charles John of Sweden at Trachenberg Castle, where a strategy was outlined that became known as the Trachenberg Plan once Austria joined the Coalition on 12 August 1813. The Coalition armies were to avoid battle with Napoleon himself, retreat whenever he advanced and target the forces of his marshals. The Army of Bohemia engaged him at Dresden on 27 August and the French won, but close adherence to the plan brought Coalition victories at Großbeeren, Kulm, Katzbach and Dennewitz.
sections.forces:
The French had around 160,000 soldiers and 700 guns, plus 10,000 Poles, 9,000 Italians and 19,000 Germans of the Confederation of the Rhine, a total of 198,000 troops. By other estimates their combined forces were up to 225,000, and the guns brought in over all four days numbered 900. The Coalition had around 380,000 troops and 1,500 guns: 145,000–150,000 Russians, 115,000 Austrians, 75,000–90,000 Prussians and from 19,000 to 23,000–30,000 Swedes. Most of Napoleon's troops were teenagers and inexperienced men conscripted after the near destruction of the army in Russia, and his cavalry was insufficient, which made it hard to scout enemy positions or watch his lines of communication.

The Coalition had four army-level commands: the Army of Bohemia under Schwarzenberg, the Army of Silesia under Blücher, the Army of Poland under Bennigsen, and the Army of the North, of Prussian, Russian and Swedish troops, under Charles John. Alexander I, Frederick William III and Francis I were present. Napoleon planned to take the offensive between the Pleiße and the Parthe. The converging rivers split the ground into four sectors, and by holding Leipzig and its bridges he could shift troops between them faster than the Allies could. Ney and Marmont defended the north, MacDonald the east, and Poniatowski and Augereau the Wachau and Liebertwolkwitz flank. Drouot was to command the main battery on the Gallows Height.
sections.course:
On 16 October the Allies attacked at Dölitz, Markkleeberg, Wachau and Liebertwolkwitz in the south. At Liebertwolkwitz Napoleon had Drouot form a grand battery of 150 guns and sent Murat in with 10,000 cavalry, but Murat's massed columns were harried by smaller Allied cavalry formations and driven back. Napoleon gained ground but could not break the Allied lines. In the north the Battle of Möckern, in which Blücher's Russian and Prussian corps fought Marmont's VI Corps, lasted well into the night, with 9,000 Allied and 7,000 French casualties and another 2,000 French prisoners. The first day ended in a draw. On 17 October there were only two actions, and the Allies received 145,000 troops against the French 14,000.

On 18 October Napoleon sent the captured Merveldt back on parole with an offer to give up the fortresses on the Oder and Vistula if he could withdraw behind the Saale, and to sign an armistice. The three monarchs declined. The Allies then attacked from all sides, encircling the French and forcing them back towards Leipzig. The bloodiest fighting was at Probstheida, where garden walls, artillery and the Imperial Guard repelled repeated Prussian and Russian assaults. 5,400 Saxons of Reynier's VII Corps defected to Charles John's army, and Württemberg cavalry also deserted. The French artillery had only 20,000 rounds left, and that night Napoleon began withdrawing across the White Elster.

The Allies learned of the evacuation at 7:00 on 19 October and attacked between 8:00 and 9:00, but Oudinot's 30,000 men fought street by street in Leipzig. At 1:00 in the afternoon the bridge over the Elster was blown while it was crowded, causing a rout.
sections.aftermath:
Estimates of the total killed, wounded or missing range from 80,000 to 110,000. Napoleon lost about 38,000 killed and wounded. In the retreat the Allies captured 15,000 able-bodied Frenchmen, 21,000 wounded or sick, 325 guns, 28 eagles, standards or colours and most of the French supply trains. Six French generals were killed, 12 wounded and 36 captured, including Lauriston and Reynier. Of a total Allied force of 360,000, approximately 54,000 were casualties: 34,000 in Schwarzenberg's Army of Bohemia, 12,000 in Blücher's Army of Silesia and about 4,000 each in the armies of Charles John and Bennigsen. Locals had difficulty disposing of the corpses, and some were still visible the following year.

The Coalition's heavy losses and exhaustion made prompt pursuit impossible, and the French retreated at a fast pace towards the Rhine. The Bavarian army tried to block them at Hanau, where the French won a minor victory. The battle ended the French Empire's presence east of the Rhine and brought Baden, Saxony and Württemberg over to the Coalition. Napoleon is quoted as telling the Senate at the year's end, "A year ago all Europe marched with us; today all Europe marches against us." The Confederation of the Rhine was dissolved and the Coalition invaded France in early 1814. Paris fell on 31 March, Napoleon abdicated on 6 April and he reached Elba on 30 May.
sections.sources:
Estimates of the numbers at Leipzig differ. The French are put at 198,000 troops, or up to 225,000 by other estimates, and the Coalition at around 380,000 or 360,000. One estimate puts the whole battle at about 560,000 soldiers and 133,000 casualties, another at 80,000 to 110,000 killed, wounded or missing. The first day's losses were approximately 30,000 for the Allies and about 25,000 for the French.

Several points rest on reports of one person’s motives. Alexander I is reported to have objected that Schwarzenberg's first plan was disastrous because it would not let the Coalition encircle Napoleon, and later events are said to have proved him correct: Blücher's attack in the north and the Russian Guard succeeded, while the Austrian action along the Pleiße failed. Charles John's slow advance on 18 October was purportedly due to news of a planned French attack on Berlin, and the Saxons' defection is explained by their esteem for him from Wagram. The blowing of the bridge had been delegated from General Dulauloy to Colonel Montfort to a corporal who did not know the planned time schedule.
sections.legacy:
Leipzig, also known as the Battle of the Nations, was the largest battle of the Napoleonic Wars, surpassing Borodino, Wagram, Jena and Auerstedt, Ulm and Dresden, and as the bloodiest, with over 400,000 rounds of artillery ammunition expended. It is called arguably the deciding battle of the wars. It was the second French army Napoleon had lost in as many years, and it severely damaged his reputation of invincibility. Prussia became one of the continent's great powers again after its severe setbacks in 1806.

In 1863, exactly 50 years after the battle, a monument to the blasting of the bridge was inaugurated in Leipzig. The 91-metre Monument to the Battle of the Nations (Völkerschlachtdenkmal), designed by Bruno Schmitz, was completed in 1913 at a cost of six million German gold marks. The Russian Memorial Church was dedicated to coincide with the hundredth anniversary and honours the Russian troops. The course of the fighting in the city is marked by numerous monuments and by 50 Apel-stones that mark important lines of the French and Allied troops. The Centennial Exhibition of 1913 was held in Breslau, now Wrocław, where its Centennial Hall was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006.

summary: From 16 to 19 October 1813 the Sixth Coalition's armies defeated Napoleon's Grande Armée at Leipzig, in the largest battle of the Napoleonic Wars. The Confederation of the Rhine was dissolved, and the Coalition invaded France in early 1814.
references: Digby Smith, The Napoleonic Wars Data Book (Greenhill, 1998)
notes: The article gives no named ancient or contemporary accounts, memoirs or archaeology, so the sources section can only describe the discrepancies and unattributed reports in the article itself; the editor may wish to add real sources.

Strengths: the article gives 198,000 French (160,000 + 10,000 + 9,000 + 19,000) and 'up to 225,000'; Coalition 'around 380,000' in Opposing forces but 'total force of 360,000' in Casualties; the lead gives 560,000 soldiers in all. Casualties: lead 133,000, Casualties section 80,000 to 110,000 (and Napoleon 38,000 killed and wounded, Allies 54,000: these do not add to either).
The first-day casualties (Allies 30,000, French 25,000) and the Möckern figures (9,000 and 7,000) are as given; the article calls the day a draw although it says the French gained slight victories.

The article says both that Reynier's Saxons defected 'during the fighting' on 18 October and, earlier, that Saxon units had defected at Großbeeren and Dennewitz; I used only the 18 October event. Its note that 'Napoleon was a lost cause' reasoning is partly narrative without attribution.

The Probstheida paragraph says a day earlier the Russians had taken most of the losses; I left this out. Also left out: Swedish jägers' casualties, Bogue's rockets at Paunsdorf, the Dölitz, Markkleeberg and Wachau detail, and Poniatowski's promotion and oath.
In the article's Conclusion the battle ended 'conclusively and decisively'; the lead says 'decisively defeated' and 'arguably, the deciding battle'. I kept 'decisively defeated' and the hedge.
The 'Legacy' sentence on the Breslau exhibition and the Centennial Hall is only loosely linked to the battle; the Hall's UNESCO listing is stated in the article without saying what it commemorates.

The 'Casualties' section calls the battle the bloodiest of the Napoleonic Wars; the quote of Napoleon to the Senate is as the article prints it, which says he said it on his return to Paris at the year's end.
